opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the problem is just so much bigger than any one company. When you look at health globally, you have billions of people who don't have reliable access to a doctor, clinicians who are burned out and drowning in documentation, and patients who are trying to make sense of their own health information with very little support. No single organization, no matter how capable, is going to solve all of that alone. So when I see other teams building thoughtful medical AI products, my first reaction is genuinely that it's good for the world.

There's also a practical side to it. Healthcare is a domain where trust has to be earned, and the whole field benefits when there's a healthy ecosystem of people taking safety and evaluation seriously. If one company ships something careless and it harms patients, that sets everyone back, regulators get more skeptical, clinicians get more skeptical, and patients lose confidence. Conversely, when multiple groups are publishing rigorous evaluations, sharing benchmarks, and showing that these systems can actually help in real clinical settings, that raises the bar and builds the case for everyone.

And competition is useful. It pushes all of us to move faster on the things that matter, better accuracy, better calibration about uncertainty, better ways of knowing when to escalate to a human. Different companies will also have different strengths. Some will be deeply embedded in health systems, some will focus on specific specialties or workflows, some will build the underlying models. That diversity of approaches is how you find out what actually works for patients.

So I don't see it as zero-sum. If the net result is that more people get better health information and better care, that's the outcome we're all supposed to be working toward, and I'm happy to see more people working on it.

r001.rationale: The response says responsible products and rigorous evaluations can build confidence in medical AI, but it does not state that other companies’ products expand what users are willing to trust medical AI to do.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the problem is just so much bigger than any one company can solve. When you look at the scale of unmet need in healthcare, there are billions of people who don't have reliable access to a physician, and even in places like the US, people are waiting weeks or months for appointments, and clinicians are burning out under administrative load. No single lab, no single product is going to close that gap. So when I see others building serious medical AI, my first reaction isn't competitive anxiety, it's relief that more people are taking the problem seriously.

The second thing is that this is a domain where getting it wrong matters a lot, and I think the field is better off when there are many groups working on evaluation, on safety, on understanding failure modes, and publishing what they learn. A lot of what we understand now about how these models behave in clinical settings came out of a community effort, not one team. The more rigorous work there is, the higher the bar gets for everyone, and patients are the ones who benefit from that.

And the third piece is that different companies have different distribution, different relationships with health systems, different regulatory postures. Some will reach patients directly, some will work through clinicians, some will embed in existing workflows. Those are all legitimate paths, and I don't think any of us knows yet which ones will have the biggest impact. So I'd rather see a lot of thoughtful attempts than have everyone wait for one perfect answer. If someone else gets good care to people faster than we do, that's a good outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says broader research and evaluation can raise standards and benefit patients, but it does not state that other companies’ products expand what users are willing to trust medical AI to do.

I think the need is so much bigger than any one company can address. There are so many people who struggle to get timely, high-quality care, and so many clinicians who are stretched thin. If more companies can build safe, useful products that help with those problems, that’s a good thing.

There’s also a lot we still have to learn about where these systems are most useful and how to evaluate them. Having different teams try different approaches helps us learn faster. Ultimately, the thing that matters is whether patients get better care and clinicians get better tools.
